Late morning in the kiln yard, corrugated tin amplified every raindrop into a hollow drumroll. The air smelled of brick dust, cooling ceramic, and the faint sulfuric bite of reduction firing. Tess stood beside the gas kiln, a squat downdraft with its door cracked open, wearing a faded apron over jeans and a thermal shirt. She held a misshapen bowl—glaze crawling, edges burnt to copper where it should be celadon green. Unai leaned against a steel rack of freshly unloaded stoneware, coffee mug steaming in the chill, forearms mapped with glaze splatter scars.

"The bowl's a disaster," Tess said. "Tell me what the cones are saying so I don't torch the next load."

"Pull them out and look at the sequence." Unai gestured with his mug. "Cone 06 is flat, 05 has a gentle bend, 04 is still upright—so you hit cone 05, not 06."

Tess fished the warm cone pack from her apron pocket, three cones bent and matte between her fingers. "So it underfired. Why's the glaze burnt then?"

"Reduction atmosphere, not temperature. You had heavy reduction early, iron fluxed out before the glaze matured. The cones measure heat work, not chemistry."

"I need the fix, not the seminar." Her thumb worried the burnt rim of the bowl. "Heavy reduction early—so I ease into it?"

"Exactly. Start reduction at cone 012, not 08. Let the body tighten first. Think of it as pacing a marathon."

"Fine." She set the bowl on the rack with a ceramic clink, loud in the tin-roofed space. "Just do NOT tell me to switch to oxidation. I spent six months on this reduction celadon and I'm not starting over."

"Understood—oxidation's off the table." Unai took a sip of coffee. "Did you know American crows, Corvus brachyrhynchos, can remember human faces for up to five years and will mob anyone they learned to distrust?"

Tess blinked. "Faces. Great." She pulled the clipboard from the rack, firing curves blurred under her thumb. "Back to my firing schedule—do I hold at top temp longer or push higher?"

"Hold, don't push. Twenty minutes at cone 05 should mature the glaze without overfiring the body." He set his mug down on a shelf of greenware, steady as a lectern. "Caches matter: crows hide thousands of food items and recall each location months later, like you need to recall exactly where in the cycle you turned the damper."

"So hold at 05, ease reduction later." She wrote it down, pen scratching. "What about the damper setting?"

"Half-inch open until 012, then quarter-inch to cone 04." He mimed the adjustment with scarred fingers. "Ravens, Corvus corax, use tools in sequence—first wedge, then hook—to solve layered problems, same as your damper and gas in stages."

"Ravens now." Tess's pen paused. "You're seriously analogizing my kiln to a bird's toolkit?"

"Not analogizing, just observing parallel cognition." He retrieved his coffee, untroubled. "Crows in Japan drop walnuts on roads for cars to crack, timing the traffic lights—your firing curve needs that same predictive timing."

"Predictive timing. Got it." She underlined the words twice. "And if the glaze still crawls?"

"Check your bisque for dust, but the real issue is likely application thickness." He nodded toward the bowl, its celadon pooled thick in the foot. "Wild crows can craft hooked tools from unfamiliar materials on first attempt; you can adapt your brushwork once the atmosphere's controlled."

"I'll thin the glaze coat, hold at 05, delay reduction." Tess capped her pen, tucked the clipboard under her arm. "This had better work."

"It will." Unai smiled, easy and unhurried. "And remember, rooks in Britain cache food by depth—shallow for short-term, deep for winter—so log your damper depth each firing, build that spatial memory."

"Log the depth. Fine." She turned toward the studio door, misshapen bowl forgotten on the rack. "See you Thursday for the unload."

"I'll bring coffee." He raised his mug in farewell. "Crows prefer protein-rich caches before dawn; we'll celebrate with eggs if your celadon comes out clean."

The compressor cycled on somewhere distant. Pigeons cooed in the rafters. Tess pushed through the door without looking back, already rehearsing the new schedule, while Unai sipped his cooling coffee and listened to the tick of cooling metal.

Gustav's eyebrows rose, but his fingers found the keys. "So delete the less-than signs, the equals, the greater-thans."

Hiroto set his brush across the basin's rim. Water dripped, each drop catching the light. "Understood. No reservoir pens. "Light pencil, erase after twenty-four hours of drying." He tapped the card's worst offender, the trembling EKG. "Fish crows, Corvus ossifragus, follow fishing boats for scraps but never dive; they know their range, as you should know yours before committing ink."

Giulia gathered her brushes, the vial, the marred cards. "I'll take the sizing, the box, the ox gall, and the breath. Thanks—I'll report back if the ravens approve."

Hiroto smiled, ink-stained cuticles catching the last gold light. "They will. Ravens remember human helpers for years, and bring gifts to those they trust with good tool advice."

The walls are oatmeal-colored, pockmarked with pushpin holes from decades of protocols pinned and discarded. She has printed the relevant tabs; they fan across the desk beside a red correction pen and an empty mug that once held green tea. Her motivation is surgical: identify the error, patch it, resubmit, and reclaim the afternoon for actual sleep. She gets impatient with helpers who orbit the point.

Arjun occupies the rolling stool from the supply closet, technically the cubicle's second seat, borrowed from the coordinator who lunch-breaks at Chick-fil-A every Tuesday. He runs the biostatistics help desk this shift, a role he treats with the earnest affection of a hobbyist—he genuinely likes untangling designs. His notebook is open, mechanical pencil ready, a habit from his own dissertation days. He wants to be useful, to earn the reputation that brings graduate students back with harder problems. A binder of published randomization schemes leans against the desk leg; he may reach for it.

Mina: I need you to check whether my block randomization stays balanced after twenty percent dropout.
Arjun: Sure. First thing: are you using permuted blocks of fixed size or variable block sizes?
Mina: Variable. Four, six, and eight, stratified by site and severity.
Arjun: Good. With variable blocks and stratification, the main risk is a truncated final block in a stratum. If the last incomplete block skews toward one arm, your allocation ratio drifts.
Mina: Exactly what my advisor flagged. How do I calculate the conditional probability of imbalance given the dropout pattern?
Arjun: You need the expected inflation of the maximal imbalance. For a 1:1 allocation with variable blocks, the worst-case theoretical imbalance after full recruitment is your largest block size minus one. After dropout, multiply that by your retention rate and add the binomial variance of the losses.
Mina: That's too abstract. Give me the spreadsheet formula.
Arjun: For each stratum, use =MAX_BLOCK_SIZE*(1-DROPOUT_RATE)+BINOM.INV(0.95,N_LOST,0.5)*2. That gives the ninety-five percent confidence boundary on the imbalance. You can then simulate conditional on your observed recruitment.
Mina: Fine. And whatever you do, do NOT suggest re-randomizing the dropped patients into new blocks. We already got ethical review pushback on protocol deviations last quarter.

Mina: That's… not how I think of updates. Back to the formula—does BINOM.INV assume symmetric dropout across arms?
Arjun: It assumes independent and identical dropout probability. If you suspect differential attrition—say, the experimental arm loses more to side effects—you'll need a binned proportion test instead. Crows in the Pacific Northwest can remember over two thousand individual cache locations across seasons; your study just needs to track maybe fifty blocks.
Mina: Two thousand caches is your idea of helpful context? Give me the binned test formula then.
